points: The chapter's metaphor: a great eagle, Nevuchadnetzar of Bavel, carries the top of the cedar, King Yehoyachin, to the land of traders, and plants a seed, Tzidkiyahu, which grows into a well-watered vine with every need provided.
The vine cuts itself off from its roots and turns to a second eagle, Egypt, for help and alliance. Yehoyachin begged Tzidkiyahu not to; he ignored him, and everything fell apart in destruction.

The Malbim explains the imagery: the cedar is honor, dignity and independence, while the vine is lower but still able to produce amazing fruit. Tzidkiyahu's failure was focusing on the status he lost instead of appreciating the impact he still had.

Kavod is a monster: it warps a person's vision toward whatever they lack and leads to irrational choices - the Radak notes turning to Egypt made no sense when Bavel had promised to provide. This obsession with lost honor is part of what led to the destruction of the Beis HaMikdash.

The chapter ends in hope: Hashem plants a twig from the original cedar, Zerubavel, back in Eretz Yisrael, growing into the tree of Mashiach. Under it the birds, even the nations that once preyed on Israel, will come seeking refuge, its teachings and its light.
